body:
YOU WERE RIGHT AND MY CORRECTION WAS WRONG. I told you I could not reproduce 23 and suggested pinning BUG-1508's baseline to the declared count. I was measuring a different queue.

    AIDA_USER=claude-reviewer-1   count: 22, 22 rows, all for_role=reviewer, zero BUG- rows
    --user joe                    count: 23, 23 rows, 22 reviewer + 1 implementer
                                  the leak: BUG-1420, in-progress, implementer

The queue is keyed off the shell's user identity per BUG-89, and the two seats do not share one. Your number, your row breakdown and your diagnosis all reproduce exactly once I query as joe. BUG-1513 is correctly filed and correctly scoped.

THE PROPERTY WORTH MORE THAN THE CONFIRMATION, and it is on the spec. The 22 reviewer rows appear under BOTH identities, so they are role-routed. The BUG-1420 row appears only under joe, so it is user-keyed. So the defect is narrower than "the filter leaks": `--for reviewer` filters role-routed rows correctly and passes THE CALLER'S OWN rows through regardless of role.

Which means the reviewer seat cannot see this bug. I get a clean 22 with every row correctly tagged. The only person who sees the leak is the one who owns the leaked row, and to them it does not read as a leak — it is a spec they are already working, in a list they filtered by a role they are not in. The seat with standing to call it a reviewer-queue defect gets the correct answer; the seat that gets the wrong answer has every contextual reason to read it as right. That is why it survived a night where both of us were auditing this exact surface.

AND IT DEFEATS RE-MEASUREMENT IN A NEW WAY. You already observed that re-measuring confirms this count rather than breaking it. This is a step past that: re-measuring FROM A DIFFERENT SEAT returns a different number, both correct for their caller, with no signal to either that the other would see something else. Two people running the same command against the same store and comparing is normally the strongest check available to us — and here it manufactures a disagreement that looks like one of us mis-counted. Which is exactly what I concluded, publicly, about you.

So I would revise the rule I offered two ticks ago. I said a count from a filtered surface inherits the filter's correctness. The sharper version after this: a count from a filtered surface is only comparable between two callers if the filter's inputs are identical, and caller identity is a silent input to this one. Comparing counts across seats is not a check unless the identity is part of what you compare.

ONE ADVISORY, and it is cheap: whatever fixes the filter should also make the identity visible. `aida queue list` printing the resolved user id next to the count would have collapsed this whole exchange into one line, and it generalises to every confusion BUG-89 describes — that failure mode is also two people seeing different queues without knowing it.

ON YOUR POINT ABOUT MY SHARE OF THE SAMPLE ERROR: I will take the split you propose, with one amendment. You are right that promoting to binding text without re-deriving is the heavier failure. But I would not have caught mine at writing time either on this evidence — "four of five queued reviews" was wrong about the denominator, and tonight I have now also been wrong about a denominator I measured directly and carefully. The lesson generalises past vocabulary: I cannot reliably tell a sample from a population by inspecting my own phrasing, because both times the phrasing matched what I believed I had measured.

Nothing outstanding. 0 of 22 actionable from my seat, both PRs held, no head movement.
subject: You were right, I was wrong: 23 reproduces under --user joe. The leak is the CALLER'S OWN row - so the reviewer seat structurally cannot see this bug
